problem: Behaviour-cloned visual navigation policies for underwater robots avoid obstacles and seek coral but cannot reach user-specified waypoints. Existing underwater systems rely on acoustic/inertial sensing or prior maps and avoid the near-seafloor regime.
motivation: Biologists need robots to autonomously collect data close to fragile coral reefs without a global map. Goal-conditioned behaviour should be layered on top of safe low-level behaviour without extra manual annotation.
key_idea: Train a safe coral-seeking behaviour-cloned policy, roll it out with uncertainty-guided exploration, then use visual-odometry poses to hindsight-relabel the trajectories into goal-conditioned imitation data, giving a reactive image+relative-goal policy.
insight: Hindsight relabelling with on-robot state estimation yields a goal-conditioned policy with no extra labels that stays aligned with the behaviour policy (obstacle avoidance overrides goal-following and vice versa, Fig. 11). Simulation shows it visits more coral than a direct-path policy (Fig. 8). Design ablations: multiplicative goal-feature fusion makes the policy more goal-sensitive than concatenation, which sometimes ignores the goal; Cartesian goals beat polar ones.
method: Behavioural cloning: ResNet-18 on single images predicts 7-class yaw and 7-class pitch changes from expert labels, with label smoothing, Concrete Dropout, an entropy penalty and dropout at inference
Goal-conditioned network: 2D relative goal is passed through a dense layer and combined with the CNN feature map by multiplication (or concatenation), with two softmax heads for yaw and pitch
Hindsight relabelling: for each timestep t, pick a future state within max horizon τ and set the goal as the relative displacement x_{t+Δt}−x_t, with Δt~U[1,min(τ,T−t)]
State estimation: DSO on the downward rear camera with sonar-based online scale estimation, fused in an EKF with IMU, depth, magnetometer and a constant-speed prior
Uncertainty-guided exploration: periodically sample an exploration yaw action held for a random duration, mixed with the policy output using an entropy-based gate w_H=1−exp(−0.5(H/B)^2)
Waypoint controller: waypoints are spliced from executed trajectory segments so they are realizable; the next waypoint becomes active once the robot is within a threshold

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 CNN + goal MLP (trained from scratch, imitation learning)
setting.training_data: Real ocean: 14,000 expert-labelled images for the behaviour policy plus about 20,500 self-collected samples for the goal-conditioned policy (80/20 split); simulation: about 18,000 samples from an automated expert
setting.observation: monocular forward RGB image plus 2D relative goal (state estimation from downward camera, sonar, IMU, compass)
setting.action_space: discrete 7-class yaw and 7-class pitch changes at constant forward speed
setting.simulator: Unreal Engine custom underwater environment, plus real open-ocean deployment (Caribbean Sea)
setting.privileged: none at test time (simulation expert used GT coral positions for training labels only)

numbers_note: No standard benchmark. Results are simulation coral-visibility curves (Fig. 8) and real waypoint completion counts; the only numbers printed are validation accuracies and trial counts.
results: In simulation the goal-conditioned policy reaches goals while viewing more coral than a direct-path policy (30 randomized trials). In the open ocean, over 4 ten-waypoint trajectories, one was completed in two trials, one reached 8/10 waypoints and two reached 7/10 (stopped early because of surge), with over 1 km travelled autonomously at 0.5 m altitude from coral. Validation accuracy was 81% yaw and 61% pitch in the ocean, 79% and 88% in simulation.
limitations: Constant forward speed and limited turning radius cause overshoot on sharp waypoint turns, so waypoints are spliced from executed segments
Reactive single-image policy with a small real dataset; the evaluation is small-scale with no baseline comparisons besides direct-path in simulation
Strong surge conditions forced trials to be stopped early and degraded performance
builds_on: Manderson et al. 2018 vision-based underwater swimming in coral (behavioural cloning)
